Houthi drone destroyed near Mecca, says Saudi-led military coalition

Houthis announced several major attacks on Saudi Arabia over the past week, including attacks on an air base, wounding 13 civilians. However, the group has denied targeting Mecca.

Reuters

16 September, 2026 12:03 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

Smoke billows into the sky in a screengrab from a video said to show Houthi fighters attacking Saudi-backed forces in the location given by the source as al Jawf governorate, Yemen, in this screengrab taken from a video released by Houthi Military Media. | Reuters

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

Cairo: Saudi Arabia’s air defences destroyed a Houthi drone south of Mecca before it entered prohibited airspace over the holy city, a spokesperson for the Saudi-led military coalition in Yemen said on Wednesday, as fighting spreads in the Middle East.

The drone, intercepted on Tuesday evening, was the second Houthi attempt to target Mecca after a ballistic missile launch in July 2017, spokesperson Turki al-Malki said in a statement, and follows a week of attacks from Iran-aligned Houthi fighters that have drawn Saudi Arabia deeper into the war.

Mecca is home to some of the holiest sites in Islam and the focal point of the annual hajj pilgrimage, and its security was a “red line,” the coalition spokesperson al-Malki said in the statement.

Show Full Article

Houthi officials have denied targeting Mecca.

The attacks on Saudia Arabia have shocked global energy markets roiled by the six-month U.S.-Iran war, which has slowed shipping through the Strait of Hormuz to a trickle.

The Houthis have seized control of parts of Yemen’s Red Sea coast in recent days overlooking the Bab el-Mandeb, one of the world’s most important shipping straits, threatening Saudi Arabia’s oil exports rerouted from the Strait of Hormuz.

Saudi Arabia issued security alerts for Mecca on Tuesday, but Houthi political bureau member Mohammed al-Farah denied the group had targeted the city, calling the allegation “an outright lie” in comments carried by the Houthi-run SABA news agency.

The Houthis have announced several major attacks on Saudi Arabia over the past week, including attacks on an air base on Monday, which they said were in retaliation for airstrikes on Yemen. The air base attack wounded 13 civilians, Saudi-led military coalition officials said.

Saudi Arabia has blamed a separate pro-Iranian movement, based in Iraq, for an attack on Friday that knocked out one of the kingdom’s most important oil transport routes, the East-West Pipeline across the Arabian desert.

The 1,200-km (745-mile) East-West Pipeline linking Saudi Arabia’s Gulf oil fields to the Red Sea has been the kingdom’s principal export route while shipping through the Strait of Hormuz has been disrupted by nearly seven months of war, which has killed thousands of people across the region.

Since the pipeline was shut after Friday’s attack, traders say a prolonged closure could cut off as much as 4% of global oil supply.

Saudi Arabia has not said when operations might resume.

But U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright told CNBC on Tuesday that crude oil should be flowing through the pipeline within days.

Saudi Arabia has led a coalition battling the Houthis since 2015. The conflict had largely quietened under a ceasefire in recent years, but reignited when the Houthis pushed back forces aligned with the Yemeni government this month.

Saudi Arabia’s Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman phoned U.S. President Donald Trump last week seeking military support, which so far has been limited to intelligence aid.

Is the China-Pakistan arms nexus exporting authoritarianism? The case of the JF-17

Arms sales to non-democratic states by like-minded regimes are a subtle yet consequential tool of extending sway. The JF-17’s export pattern fits this description closely

Bantirani Patro

16 September, 2026 11:34 am IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

Illustration: Shruti Naithani/ThePrint

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

W hen the Pakistan Air Force released a mostly AI-generated video on September 7 depicting its implausible ‘victory’ over India during Operation Sindoor, it grabbed eyeballs and got mocked.

But beneath the fabricated claims lay a genuine defence upgrade.

For the first time, Pakistan showcased its Chinese-origin HQ-17AE short-range surface-to-air missile (SAM) system, and Turkish-made Şahin counter-unmanned aerial vehicle (C-UAV) weapon and Korkut self-propelled anti-aircraft gun (SPAAG).

Show Full Article

This display reinforced the obvious — Islamabad’s deepening defence partnerships with Beijing and Ankara. But it also pointed to something subtler and larger: a pattern of growing defence cooperation between autocratic governments and the role the military-industrial complex plays in entrenching such illiberalism. Nowhere is this trend clearer than in the export story of the JF-17 Thunder fighter jet, which also featured in the PAF video.

Also Read: Asim Munir wants to redraw Pakistan. The first field marshal’s One Unit debacle offers a warning

The ‘thunder’ around JF-17 From December 2025 onwards, Reuters began publishing a string of reports, almost like clockwork, about Pakistan signing or negotiating defence deals with several countries. At the heart of these deals was the JF-17 fighter jet. Libya was the first to be reported on. Bangladesh, Saudi Arabia, Sudan, Indonesia and Somalia have since reportedly expressed interest in acquiring the aircraft.

The noise around the JF-17 ‘Thunder’ petered out a few months into 2026. But such prospective deals hold pieces of a larger puzzle that could aid understanding of the broader alignment between China, Pakistan and the states operating, or interested in, the aircraft.

Jointly produced by the Pakistan Aeronautical Complex and Chengdu Aircraft Corporation, the JF-17 is powered by Russian-made Klimov engines: RD-93 (used in Block I and Block II variants) and RD-93MA (Block III). With its first prototype taking its maiden flight in 2003 and later being inducted into the Pakistan Air Force in the late 2000s, the JF-17 has been elevated to what can be regarded as a tour de force of the China-Pakistan friendship —  dubbed “higher than the mountains…stronger than steel”.

While the sudden surge in interest from late 2025 did raise eyebrows about the substance of Reuters ’ reports, the JF-17 does appear to be having its moment under the sun. Materialisation of deals notwithstanding, the reports alone amounted to a huge publicity boost. Coupled with the fact that the JF-17 now has the tag of ‘ combat-tested ’ after Pakistan reportedly used the aircraft, alongside the Chinese J-10Cs, during its four-day conflict with India in May 2025. That it was deployed against an air force operating a mix of Western and Russian fighter planes lent further credibility to the aircraft’s prowess.

A tool of influence What is underexplored about this 4.5-generation, single-engine, all-weather, multi-role aircraft is the profile of its current and speculated export destinations. Beijing appears to be leveraging the JF-17 as a tool to export its influence, specifically among nations that are at odds, to varying degrees, with the largely liberal West.

Libya is a case in point. Pakistan’s deal was signed with the Libyan National Army, whose authority over eastern Libya is not recognised by the United Nations, which only accords legitimacy to the government in charge of the western territory. Add to that, Libya has been subject to an arms embargo since 2011, with arms transfers allowed solely to the internationally recognised government in Tripoli. Similarly, Sudan, a country rendered asunder by the civil war that erupted in 2023, is subject to arms embargoes by the West.

The political trajectories of the three countries that officially operate the JF-17 tell a similar story. Myanmar, Nigeria and Azerbaijan have displayed weakened democratic principles to differing degrees and have increasingly taken an authoritarian turn. Myanmar, the first importer of the JF-17, is sanctioned by the US and some of its allies to boot, while the country itself has been ravaged by a civil war since 2021.

This suggests the Sino-Pakistani nexus is consolidating influence among nations with governance and freedom profiles similar to theirs through inter alia defence partnerships. China’s export of its authoritarianism in digital and political forms is fairly well-documented. Less examined is the role of defence exports. Arms sales to non-democratic, authoritarian or military-dominated states by like-minded regimes account for a subtler yet consequential tool of extending sway. The JF-17’s export pattern fits this description closely.

While Pakistan’s former army chief Qamar Javed Bajwa pivoted from geopolitics to geoeconomics , his successor, Field Marshal Asim Munir, seems to be advancing what can be called a mix of economics and defence.

Pakistan is projecting JF-17 deals as a means of generating revenue for its economy, which has a long-standing history of external bailouts. Defence Minister Khawaja Asif remarked that the country is “receiving so many orders that Pakistan may not need the International Monetary Fund in six months”. Further highlighting this defence-economics nexus is the potential conversion of a Saudi loan into an arms agreement. That the military, not the civilian leadership, is steering such efforts is evident; for example, Field Marshals Asim Munir of Pakistan and Khalifa Haftar of Libya are negotiating the JF-17 deal.

China: The ultimate winner? A Foreign Affairs essay, ‘ The Illiberal International’ , spotlighted the burgeoning coordination among illiberal governments through military and financial tools, resulting in the entrenchment of illiberal governance.

To illustrate this, the piece cites Turkey’s supply of Bayraktar TB2 drones to Azerbaijan and Libya — both of which have also cut JF-17 deals with Pakistan. One can also reference the Turkey-Pakistan defence partnership in a similar vein. Turkey plans to establish a drone assembly facility in Pakistan. Here, it is worth mentioning that just as Pakistan is maximising the JF-17’s battlefield credentials to buoy up the aircraft’s marketability, Turkey has similarly capitalised on its drone’s performance in the Russia-Ukraine and Armenia-Azerbaijan conflicts to boost its exportability.

A separate Lowy Institute study identifies four ways through which military and security cooperation occurs among illiberal powers: transfer of weapons and war-fighting equipment; provision of non-lethal resources like intelligence and satellite information; structured military exercises; and, more prominently, through formal pacts. China and Pakistan tick all four of these boxes and may extend the same channels of cooperation to countries they want as customers.

The Mecca Joint Defense Agreement between Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan, all three of which have illiberal governments, also checks the same four boxes. China stands to gain from this indirectly. As Pakistan becomes more embedded in Gulf security arrangements, Chinese-built systems, training and maintenance networks could gain a  foothold   in the region by extension, given China’s overwhelming influence over Pakistan. There can also be an overlap of defence supply chains and the military-industrial complex of the Mecca Pact countries and China. If collaboration between them deepens, the role of a ‘liberal’ US as a traditional security guarantor in the region will further diminish, paving the way for a Chinese-led ‘illiberal’ architecture.

China, despite co-producing the JF-17, does not itself operate the aircraft. But Beijing is unmistakably the face of such deals and any sale is likely to be regarded as a win for Chinese influence, which China may well be encouraging.

There is reason to believe this. The states operating or planning to negotiate a JF-17 deal are  participants  in China’s Belt and Road Initiative (BRI), already tied to Beijing economically, infrastructurally, and to some extent, through a political slant. It is not implausible that Beijing sees defence cooperation as a way of deepening the extant relationship. Correlation is not causation. But a history of economic cooperation often facilitates future collaboration in other sectors.

Many of these countries are also mired in conflicts, domestic and international, which drives their increased need for arms procurement. In an unstable geopolitical environment, the Sino-Pakistani military-industrial complex stands to benefit from conflict-prone regions, where their platforms can acquire the combat-proven tag, boosting future sales. The more battlefields their platforms are tested in, the better.

And where there is war, there is money to be made, as the saying goes. Africa, convulsed by conflicts that get little attention due to the high-profile wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, is one region worth watching closely on this front. China and Pakistan, and even Turkey, may seek to make Africa their next big market for weapons.

Also read: Saudi firm bets $200 mn on Afghanistan’s energy sector. Can it succeed where Chinese failed?

Arms and ideology The intertwining of ideology and defence exports is not new, but it is often overlooked.

As China throws its weight globally, its growing role in the weapons market, especially among countries classified as illiberal, deserves closer scrutiny from observers and policymakers. Such deals are not purely confined to the defence sphere. They also signal deeper strategic alignment, something defenders of liberal democracies would do well to examine if they want to halt the expansion of illiberal networks.

Part of the appeal is that Beijing, unlike Washington, does not impose political, value-based constraints on defence partnerships. A sense of ease appears to exist between China and countries that have either not reaped the benefits from a democratic system or are seeking to diversify partnerships beyond the West, both of which pave the way for greater trust. Such relations not only entrench China’s influence within these states, but in a way also sustain those illiberal regimes.

For Pakistan, if these deals materialise, its cherished goal of becoming a net security provider in the Arab region and beyond could inch closer to reality, with the already existing Strategic Mutual Defense Agreement (SDMA) with Saudi Arabia and the Mecca Agreement acting as two anchors.

Bantirani Patro is a staff writer at ThePrint. She tweets @bantirani_patro. Views are personal.

(Edited by Asavari Singh)

‘Bereft of logic’: Delhi HC’s earful to ITAT over orders, handling of Patanjali income tax appeals

The court set aside all 7 orders and restored the matters for fresh consideration before a different ITAT bench, making clear that it had not expressed opinion on merits of the tax dispute.

Aditya Edara

16 September, 2026 10:51 am IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

Representational image | Reuters

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

New Delhi: The Delhi High Court has quashed all seven orders passed by the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT) in tax appeals involving Patanjali Ayurved Limited, flagging what it called a “shocking picture” of procedural lapses and expressing strong displeasure over the manner in which the tribunal handled the cases.

A bench of Justices Dinesh Mehta and Rajneesh Kumar Gupta said the ITAT order reflected “non-application of mind” and “undue haste”, besides being “bereft of any logic, reasoning or rationale”. The court also referred to a “procedural lacuna” and said the tribunal members had shown “undue haste rather recklessness” in passing and signing the order.

The appeals before the high court were filed by the income tax department, with Patanjali as the respondent. The revenue department challenged the ITAT orders that had earlier granted relief to Patanjali in four appeals.

Show Full Article

The high court set aside all seven orders and restored the matters for fresh consideration before a different ITAT bench, while making clear that it had not expressed any opinion on the merits of the tax dispute.

Four appeals heard, pronounced in a day The procedural issue arose from the manner in which the seven appeals were disposed of by the tribunal. Four appeals filed by Patanjali ITA 534 to 537/Del/2025 concerning assessment years 2013-14 to 2015-16 and 2017-18, were heard and pronounced on 6 August 2025.

Three cross-appeals filed by the revenue department ITA 605 to 607/Del/2025 showed 13 August 2025 as both the date of hearing and date of pronouncement.

Despite the different dates, a common order was passed on 13 August on the cross-appeals filed by the opposites sides. The high court asked how one order could cover appeals heard and pronounced a week apart. The court also noted that the ITAT order contained fewer than seven paragraphs. It clarified that the brevity was not the issue, but the lack of reasoning and application of mind was.

Also Read: Patanjali told to recall 4 tonnes of red chilli powder from market, but no public alert by FSSAI

Assessments challenged before ITAT The seven appeals arose from a search action conducted between 31 October and 3 November 2018, which led to proceedings under Section 153C of the Income Tax Act.

Section 153C enables the tax authorities to assess a person other than the person searched where material found during the search is considered relevant to that person.

The proceedings ultimately culminated in assessment orders dated 27 March 2023. These were subsequently challenged before the Commissioner of Income Tax (Appeals), whose orders passed in November and December 2024 were then taken before the ITAT. The ITAT quashed the four assessments challenged by Patanjali and dismissed the three cross appeals.

ITAT finding challenged  The income tax department then approached the high court against the ITAT orders.

The judgement records that the revenue department’s senior standing counsel Puneet Rai contended that the ITAT had treated the assessment years as “unabated” after the assessing officer issued the Section 153C notice on 6 August 2021, while rejecting the revenue department’s contention on the issue.

The judgement did not decide the appeal on merits. Instead, the high court focused on the procedural defects in the ITAT order. It said the order was “bereft of any logic, reasoning or rationale” and criticised the tribunal members for showing “undue haste rather recklessness” while passing and signing it.

All seven orders set aside The high court said it had “no other option” but to set aside all seven ITAT orders and restore the appeals to their original numbers for fresh adjudication.

The matters will be heard by a different ITAT bench. The court also directed that a copy of its order be sent to the ITAT president and the secretary of the law and justice ministry.

The court clarified that it had made no observation on the merits of the tax dispute. The fresh ITAT bench will therefore be free to examine the issues and take an independent view.

Aditya is an alum of ThePrint School of Journalism, interning with ThePrint.

(Edited by Nardeep Singh Dahiya)

US just accelerated space arms race. What Air Force Secy said about ‘on-orbit space control weapons’

In a move that could accelerate an arms race with Russia and China in Earth’s orbit, the US has confirmed, for the first time, that it has deployed weapons in space.

Ashwin Shekhar

16 September, 2026 06:30 am IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

File photo of US Space Force Guardians assigned to Space Delta 5 monitor computer workstations at Vandenberg Space Force Base, California, on 18 December, 2025 | David Dozoretz/US Space Forces | Handout via Reuters

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

New Delhi: The US has deployed satellites with strike capabilities in Earth’s orbit, Air Force Secretary Troy E. Meink said on Monday, in the first such public acknowledgment by the US military.

Speaking at the 2026 Air and Space Cyber Conference in Maryland, Meink said, “We are increasing readiness against existing threats, and the United States has on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the Joint Force against hostile adversary action.” Meink did not disclose the type of weapons involved or when they were deployed.

The revelation comes amid growing tensions in space involving Russia and China, as the two major military powers increasingly develop capabilities to operate and potentially fight in space.

Show Full Article

Space has also become more critical to modern warfare. Battlefield AI and military infrastructure rely heavily on Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) data, making space an increasingly important domain for strategic defence.

The US and India have traditionally demonstrated anti-satellite (ASAT) capabilities through ground-launched missiles. In March 2019, India’s Mission Shakti used a modified Prithvi Defence Vehicle Mark-2 (PDV MK2) interceptor to destroy the defunct Microsat-E satellite in Low Earth Orbit (LEO). The test was conducted from the APJ Abdul Kalam Island in Odisha.

On the other hand, Russia reportedly operates manoeuvrable “stalker” satellites, including Cosmos 2558, which has been capable of shadowing critical targets such as the commercial ICEYE-X36 satellite supporting Ukrainian intelligence.

China has also expanded its military space capabilities. Its Shijian-21 (SJ-21) satellite is equipped with robotic arms that can physically manoeuvre other satellites into so-called graveyard orbits, where they are effectively removed from operational use.

The militarisation of space dates back to the 1950s, when the US and Soviet Union began competing to develop capabilities to destroy satellites. The 1967 Outer Space Treaty subsequently prohibited the placement of weapons of mass destruction in orbit.

The treaty, however, does not amount to a blanket ban on military activity in space. Russia drew international criticism after destroying one of its defunct satellites in orbit during a ground-based ASAT missile test, creating a large amount of orbital debris.

China criticised the latest US disclosure, with its foreign ministry accusing Washington of “preparing for war in outer space” and warning against turning space “into a battlefield, as well as an arms race there”.

Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov also reacted to the development and called for “the complete demilitarisation of space”.

Ashwin Shekhar is an alum of ThePrint School of Journalism, currently interning with ThePrint.

(Edited by Chingkheinganbi Mayengbam)
